catalog_quote: Kipangwa is not a tonal language different from many Bantu languages (Hyman, 1976; Kisseberth & Odden, 2003). Instead, Kipangwa features a regular penultimate accent. This characteristic is also observed in the neighbouring language, Vwanji G66 (Eaton, 2019). In Kipangwa, stress is realised on the penultimate syllable of a word. However, words are frequently put together as a prosodic entity in the sense that the penultimate syllable of the rightmost word receives more pronounced stress as in (5) and (6). (5) avanu ˈava ... 'these children' (6) ifideko ˈfyangu ... 'my chairs' In (5) and (6), the penultimate syllables of demonstrative ˈava 'these' and that of possessive ˈfyangu 'my' receive the more pronounced stress. However, in this paper, no further attempt is made to mark stress in examples in order to maintain consistency with the data found in written texts.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Kipangwa has no lexical tone; every word carries a regular penultimate accent (stress on the second-to-last syllable). Within a prosodic group (e.g. noun + demonstrative/possessive) the penultimate syllable of the rightmost word is the most prominent, e.g. avanu ˈava 'these people', ifideko ˈfyangu 'my chairs'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed; only relative prominence between word-level penults inside a prosodic group (rightmost strongest).
new_statements.exceptions: None mentioned. Authors note vowel length is contrastive (short/long) and long vowels never occur word-finally; they do not mark stress in their examples beyond (5)-(6).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('penultimate syllable of a word'), plus an explicit phrase-level statement that phrasal prominence falls on the penult of the rightmost word. Examples are short NPs elicited from 18 native speakers in Ludewa District and Kipangwa Bible storybooks; no instrumental data. The paragraph is a 2-page structural sketch inside a morphosyntax article, not a dedicated phonology.
new_statements.identity_note: Kipangwa = Pangwa [pbr], glottocode pang1287, Guthrie G64 (Mtega 2023 mislabels it G65), spoken in Ludewa District, Njombe Region; the JULACE data come from 18 informants in Ludewa District plus Kipangwa Bible storybooks and are not assigned to a named dialect. Riegg 2021 (citing SIL 2003) notes several mutually intelligible dialects. No separate dialect glottocodes exist.
